short: The Buddhist teaching that everything arises in dependence on conditions, with no independent, self-caused existence.
beginner: Dependent origination means nothing exists on its own: everything comes into being because of other things. Buddhism uses this to explain how suffering arises and how it can stop.
what: Pratityasamutpada ('arising in dependence') is the Buddhist account of causality. In its classic form it is a chain of twelve links, from ignorance through formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the senses, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming and birth to ageing and death. Seeing this chain explains the arising of suffering without positing a permanent self, and reversing it describes the path to cessation. Later schools interpret it differently.
scholar: Early texts state the principle as: when this is, that is; from the arising of this, that arises. Abhidharma schools analyse it in terms of momentary dharmas. Nagarjuna's Mulamadhyamakakarika identifies dependent origination with emptiness (shunyata): because things arise dependently they lack svabhava (own-being). Yogacara reads it through consciousness and its seeds. Hindu critics, especially Nyaya and Vedanta, argue that such a chain requires a lasting subject or ground.

perspectives.view: Theravada presents the twelve links as a description of how rebirth and suffering continue across lives and moment to moment, and meditative insight into it as liberating.
For Nagarjuna, whatever arises dependently is empty of own-being; dependent origination and emptiness are two ways of saying the same thing.
Yogacara explains the chain through the storehouse consciousness (alaya-vijnana), in which karmic seeds ripen as experience.

follow.note: The Buddha's teaching on the conditioned arising of suffering.
The chain explains how dukkha arises and ceases.
Dependent origination explains continuity without a permanent self.
Nagarjuna equates dependent origination with emptiness.
The foundational Madhyamaka text on this equation.
Contrast: Nyaya argues for an enduring self as the substrate of experience.
